prereq: Comfort with simple algebra and iterative updates

symbols: state, action at time t, and the reward that follows it
policy: probability of taking action a in state s
value of state s: expected long-run reward from s
exploration rate: probability of a random move

sections.title: What reinforcement learning is and when to use it
sections.plain: Learning what to do from rewards, by trying things.
sections.body:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning how to map situations to actions so as to maximise a numerical reward signal. The learner is not told which action is correct; it must discover which actions yield the most reward by trying them. RL is best thought of as an approach to a class of problems (sequential decision-making from feedback), not as a particular network or algorithm.

A widely used industry definition: RL is a type of machine learning in which an agent learns to perform a task through repeated trial-and-error interactions with a dynamic environment, guided by rewards.

When RL is a good fit.
  • A model of the environment is known but has no analytic solution (e.g. a complex scheduling system).
  • Only a simulation of the environment is available (robotics, games, logistics).
  • The only way to learn about the environment is to interact with it (recommendation, online advertising, control).

When a labelled "right answer" exists for every input, supervised learning is usually simpler and more data-efficient.

sections.title: RL vs supervised and unsupervised learning
sections.plain: Supervised learns from answers, unsupervised from structure, RL from consequences.
sections.body:
SupervisedUnsupervisedReinforcement
Learns fromLabelled examples (x, y)Unlabelled data xInteraction: rewards for actions taken
DataFixed dataset given up frontFixed datasetGenerated by the agent's own behaviour
Typical problemsClassification, regressionClustering, association, density estimationControl, games, sequential decisions
SupervisionThe correct answerNoneAn evaluative scalar, often delayed
AlgorithmsLinear/logistic regression, SVM, trees, neural netsk-means, PCA, AprioriQ-learning, SARSA, policy gradients, DQN, PPO
AimGeneralise the mapping x → yDiscover hidden structureMaximise long-run cumulative reward
Instructive vs evaluative feedback. Supervised learning says "the answer was B"; RL only says "you scored 3". The agent cannot tell from 3 alone whether another action would have scored 10, which is why it must explore.

sections.title: Characteristics of RL problems
sections.plain: No teacher, decisions in sequence, time matters, and feedback arrives late.
sections.body:
1. No supervisor, only a reward signal. Nobody labels the best action.
  2. Sequential decision making. Actions change the state, so they change what the agent sees and can do next; data are not i.i.d.
  3. Time really matters. The order of experience is part of the problem.
  4. Delayed feedback. A move's consequence (e.g. losing a game) may appear many steps later.
The credit-assignment problem. When a reward finally arrives, which of the many earlier actions deserve credit or blame? Values (expected long-run reward) and temporal-difference updates are RL's main tools for propagating late feedback back to early decisions.

RL also faces the exploration–exploitation trade-off: to obtain reward the agent should exploit actions known to be good, but to find such actions it must explore actions it has not tried.

sections.title: The agent–environment loop
sections.plain: See the state, act, receive a reward and the next state, repeat.
sections.body:
The agent is the learner and decision maker; the environment is everything outside it. At each discrete time step $t = 0, 1, 2, \dots$:

$$S_t \xrightarrow{\ \text{agent chooses}\ } A_t \xrightarrow{\ \text{environment returns}\ } R_{t+1},\ S_{t+1}$$

producing a trajectory $S_0, A_0, R_1, S_1, A_1, R_2, S_2, \dots$. The reward for the action taken at time $t$ is written $R_{t+1}$ because it arrives together with the next state.

  • State $S_t$: the information the agent uses to decide (board position, sensor readings).
  • Action $A_t$: what the agent does (move a piece, apply torque).
  • Reward $R_{t+1} \in \mathbb R$: a scalar the agent tries to maximise in the long run.

The boundary between agent and environment is drawn where the agent's control ends, not where its body ends: a robot's motors and sensors are usually part of the environment.

sections.title: Elements of RL: policy, reward, value, model
sections.plain: How to act, what is good now, what is good in the long run, and how the world responds.
sections.body:
ElementWhat it isEveryday analogue
Policy $\pi(a\mid s)$Mapping from states to actions or action probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)=\Pr(A_t=a\mid S_t=s)$Habit or reflex
Reward signalImmediate scalar feedback defining the goalPleasure or pain
Value functionExpected total future reward from a state (or state–action pair)Judgement: "this position is promising"
Model (optional)Predicts next state and reward given state and actionImagination, used for planning

Rewards are given by the environment; values must be estimated from experience, and most RL algorithms are really methods for estimating values efficiently. Actions are chosen on the basis of value judgements: we seek states of highest value, not highest immediate reward.

Model-based methods use a model to plan; model-free methods learn values or policies directly from trial and error.

sections.title: Tic-tac-toe with a value table
sections.plain: Store a win probability for every board, mostly pick the best next board, sometimes try a random one.
sections.body:
Against an imperfect opponent, classical minimax (which assumes optimal play) cannot exploit mistakes. An RL player instead keeps a table with one number per board state: the current estimate of the probability of winning from that state.

  • Initialise: boards with three X's in a row → 1; boards with three O's in a row or full (draw) → 0; all others → 0.5.
  • Greedy move (most of the time): pick the move leading to the board with the highest value.
  • Exploratory move (occasionally, with probability ε): pick a random move, to discover boards whose values are wrong.
  • After each greedy move, back up the value of the earlier state toward the later one.
$$V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\,\big[V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)\big]$$

Worked step. A board has $V(s)=0.5$; the greedy move leads to a winning board $V(s')=1$; with $\alpha = 0.1$: $V(s) \leftarrow 0.5 + 0.1\,(1-0.5) = 0.55$. Repeated over many games, the values converge toward the true win probabilities against this opponent, and the greedy policy becomes strong. Exploratory moves are not backed up (they would teach the value of a random move, not of good play).

Code example ex1 trains this player against a random opponent: greedy win rate rises from 87% to over 99% within 20,000 games while the table grows to about 2,100 states.

sections.title: The temporal-difference rule and the step size
sections.plain: Move the estimate a fraction α toward a better target; α controls speed vs stability.
sections.body:
The tic-tac-toe rule is the simplest temporal-difference (TD) method: it learns from the difference between estimates at two successive times. It is an instance of the update that recurs throughout RL:

$$\text{NewEstimate} \leftarrow \text{OldEstimate} + \alpha\,\big[\text{Target} - \text{OldEstimate}\big]$$

The bracket is an error; α decides how much of it to correct.

Choice of αBehaviour
Reduced over time toward 0 (e.g. $1/n$)Converges to the true values for a stationary opponent/environment
Reduced but never to 0Keeps tracking slow changes in the opponent
ConstantAdapts fastest to change, but estimates keep fluctuating with noise

Code example ex2: a hidden value jumps from 2 to 5. The sample average ($\alpha=1/n$) is still at 3.49 at the end; constant $\alpha=0.1$ reaches 4.83 within 100 samples and has mean error 0.21 after the jump.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Reward ≠ value. A chess capture may give immediate material but lose the game; values account for what follows.
  • RL is not just deep RL. Tabular methods like the tic-tac-toe player are RL with no neural network at all; deep RL replaces the table with a network when states are too many.
  • Exploration costs something. Every random move is a move not spent winning; later sessions (bandits) quantify this trade-off.
  • Evolutionary methods could also learn tic-tac-toe by evaluating whole policies over many games, but they ignore which states were visited during a game; value-based RL uses that information.

code.title: Step size: sample average vs constant α
code.explain: Tracks a value that jumps from 2.0 to 5.0 using new = old + α(sample − old) with α = 1/n, 0.1 and 0.01.
mistakes: Choosing α so large that noise dominates.
code.notes: This same update reappears as the incremental bandit estimate (M2), TD(0) (M8) and stochastic gradient descent (M9).
code.code:
"""The step size alpha in  new = old + alpha * (target - old).

A sample average (alpha = 1/n) converges for a fixed target but adapts slowly when the
target drifts; a constant alpha keeps tracking a moving target. Here a hidden 'true value'
jumps from 2.0 to 5.0 halfway through, and noisy samples arrive one at a time.
"""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
T = 2000
true = np.where(np.arange(T) < T // 2, 2.0, 5.0)
samples = true + rng.normal(0, 1, T)

def track(alpha_fn):
    est, out = 0.0, []
    for n, x in enumerate(samples, start=1):
        est += alpha_fn(n) * (x - est)
        out.append(est)
    return np.array(out)

runs = {"1/n (sample average)": track(lambda n: 1 / n),
        "constant 0.1": track(lambda n: 0.1),
        "constant 0.01": track(lambda n: 0.01)}
print(f"{'rule':<22}{'est @999':>10}{'est @1100':>11}{'est @1999':>11}{'mean |err| 2nd half':>21}")
for k, e in runs.items():
    print(f"{k:<22}{e[999]:10.3f}{e[1100]:11.3f}{e[1999]:11.3f}{np.abs(e[1000:] - 5).mean():21.3f}")
print("\nalpha -> 0 (1/n): converges when nothing changes but lags after the jump;")
print("constant alpha: never fully settles (noise), but follows change; smaller = smoother but slower.")
